teaser: A beam of light, a pointing hand, and five men at a table who have not all noticed yet.
review_notes:
Scorsese: he has said in interviews (notably to Andrew Graham-Dixon) that the bar scenes of Mean Streets were modeled on Caravaggio and specifically on The Calling of Saint Matthew; wording paraphrased, please verify.
Contract of July 1599 for 400 scudi for the two side paintings; canvases in place in 1600.
X-rays showing Saint Peter was added over an earlier arrangement.
Chapel lights at San Luigi dei Francesi are coin-operated (true in recent years, check it is still the case).
Window panes described as oiled paper rather than glass.
The debate over which figure is Matthew (bearded man vs. bowed youth) is real; the traditional reading is the bearded man.
Size about 322 x 340 cm.

lesson.text: In 1973 Martin Scorsese filmed small-time gangsters in a red-lit New York bar for Mean Streets. He has said where the idea of those scenes came from: a painting of men around a table in a dim room, interrupted by someone at the door. The painting was this one, made in Rome in 1600 by a 28-year-old known as Caravaggio.

It is easy to see what a film director found here. The picture is enormous, about 3.2 by 3.4 meters (roughly 10.5 by 11 feet), and nearly half of it is empty darkness. The actors are life-size. And the light does what a spotlight does on a set: it picks out faces and lets everything else fall away.

The subject comes from the Gospels. Matthew, also called Levi, is a tax collector, a profession people despised. Jesus walks past his counting table and says two words: “Follow me.” Matthew gets up and goes. Caravaggio paints the second before he stands, when the words have landed but nobody has moved.

The chapel was paid for by a French cardinal named Matthieu Cointrel, Matteo Contarelli in Italian, who wanted scenes from the life of his name saint. He died in 1585 and the walls stayed bare for years. Caravaggio got the contract in 1599, his first big public job.

So where is Jesus? Most painters would put him in the center, glowing. Caravaggio pushes him to the far right edge, mostly in shadow, half hidden behind another man. What crosses the room is the light, and it travels in the same direction as his arm. Follow that path across the canvas.
The scene is organized by a few straight paths that all run from right to left.

lines.label: The edge of the beam
lines.text: Light enters above Christ's head and cuts the wall diagonally. It does not come from the window, whose panes stay dull. Its source is outside the picture, on Christ's side.

lines.label: The call
lines.text: Christ's arm stretches under the beam and his hand hangs loosely at the end. Extend the gesture and it lands on the lit faces at the table.

lines.label: Three hands
lines.text: Christ points. Below him Saint Peter repeats the gesture more timidly. Across the room a bearded man points too, as if asking “who, me?” The question travels by hands.

lines.label: Two worlds
lines.text: Left of this line, velvet sleeves, feathered hats and a sword: Rome in 1600. Right of it, two barefoot men in plain ancient robes. The call crosses from one time into the other.

lesson.text: That limp hand at the end of Christ's arm is a quotation. A century earlier, on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel a short walk away, Michelangelo painted God giving life to Adam. Adam's hand hangs in just this way. Caravaggio, whose first name was also Michelangelo, borrows it: this call is a second creation.

Now the table. Five men, and for 400 years everyone agreed which one is Matthew. Then some scholars began to doubt, and the argument is still open. The picture gives you the evidence for both sides. Judge for yourself.

lesson.title: Who is Matthew?
lesson.text: Three suspects sit on the left side of the table.

spots.title: The bearded man
spots.text: He looks straight toward Christ, eyes wide, with light full on his face. This is the traditional Matthew: the man who has heard and is about to answer.

spots.title: His finger
spots.text: Is he pointing at his own chest, or past himself at the young man beside him? The angle of the hand allows both. Everything in the debate hangs on this finger.

spots.title: The bowed youth
spots.text: Head down, he keeps counting coins and has noticed nothing. Some think he is Matthew, a moment before he looks up. On that reading the picture shows the last second of his old life.

spots.title: The spectacles
spots.text: An old man in a fur collar leans in and holds his glasses to his nose to inspect the money. He looks very hard, at the wrong thing.

lesson.text: Caravaggio does not show Matthew getting up. He stops the story on the instant of hesitation, and leaves the decision hanging in front of you.

Notice how differently the five men react. Two keep counting. Two boys turn toward the strangers, one leaning back, the other twisting on his stool with his sword swinging behind him. The same event reaches each person at a different speed. Caravaggio watched this happen in real card games and taverns.

He made no careful preparatory drawings, as far as anyone knows. He painted straight onto the canvas from live models and changed his mind as he went. X-rays suggest Saint Peter was squeezed in late, on top of an earlier arrangement.

With all this street realism, you may wonder what tells you the thin man on the right is divine at all. No angels, no clouds, no golden glow. Caravaggio allows himself one conventional sign, and makes it as discreet as he can.
There is exactly one supernatural mark in this room. Where is it?

spots.title: The halo
spots.text: A hairline of gold floats above Christ's head, barely brighter than the shadow around it. In a picture this large it is almost nothing. Without it, he is a man who has walked into a tax office.

lesson.text: This near absence of the sacred shocked and thrilled Rome. Saints with dirty feet in a room like the one down the street: some churchmen found it vulgar, and Caravaggio had other paintings refused for that reason. But crowds came, and young painters from all over Europe started copying the dark rooms and the hard light.

The painting has never left the wall it was made for, in the church of San Luigi dei Francesi. The chapel is dark, and visitors drop a coin into a box to switch the lights on for a minute or two. You pay a small coin to see a tax collector being called away from his coins.

One more thing about that wall. The Calling hangs on the left side of the chapel, so the real altar and its window are to the right of the canvas. The painted beam arrives from that same side. Seen in place, the light of the story seems to enter from the actual church.

The strong contrast of deep shadow and sharp light that Caravaggio made famous has a name: chiaroscuro, Italian for “light-dark.” Here it is more than a style. The light is the call itself, crossing the room.

quiz.question: Where does the main beam of light come from?
options: From the window in the back wall
From a candle on the table
From outside the picture, on Christ's side
quiz.explanation: The window panes stay dull; the beam enters from the right, above Christ.

quiz.question: Which earlier work does Christ's hanging hand quote?
options: Michelangelo's Adam on the Sistine ceiling
A Roman statue of an emperor
quiz.explanation: The limp hand copies Adam's in Michelangelo's Creation of Adam.

quiz.question: What was Matthew's job before he was called?
quiz.explanation: Matthew, also called Levi, collected taxes.

quiz.question: Why do some scholars think the bowed young man is Matthew?
options: The bearded man's finger may be pointing at him
quiz.explanation: The pointing finger can be read as aimed at the youth beside him.

quiz.question: What is the only supernatural sign in the picture?
options: A thin gold halo above Christ
A glowing book on the table
quiz.explanation: A hairline halo is the single conventional sacred sign.

quiz.question: How are the men at the table dressed?
options: In the fashions of Rome around 1600
quiz.explanation: They wear velvet, feathers and a sword, the clothes of Caravaggio's own day.

facts.text: The painting still hangs in the chapel it was painted for.
facts.explanation: It has never left San Luigi dei Francesi in Rome.

facts.text: Caravaggio placed Christ in the bright center of the composition.
facts.explanation: Christ stands at the far right edge, mostly in shadow.

facts.text: Chiaroscuro means a strong contrast between light and shadow.
